title: Clearing the Air: Health, Inequality and the Government's Role
label: 14 Sep 2026 · Air pollution evidence
summary: The Environmental Audit Committee questioned Dame Diana Johnson (Public Health Minister), Professor Sir Chris Whitty (Chief Medical Officer) and Simon Reeve (DHSC deputy director) about air pollution's health impacts, cross-government coordination, inequality, monitoring, and public messaging. The panel agreed air pollution causes around 30,000 deaths a year and much ill health, with progress made but much more to do—especially on indoor pollution, agriculture, and helping the most vulnerable. Tensions emerged over whether the Government should do more public awareness campaigning and whether UK limits lag WHO guidelines.

chapters.title: Welcome and Introductions
chapters.takeaway: The committee opened the session, noted the absence of the housing department, and heard the witnesses introduce themselves.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Today we're looking at air quality and the Government's response. Later we'll hear from Transport and DEFRA, but first we have Dame Diana Johnson and colleagues from Health. I'm disappointed that the Ministry of Housing haven't sent anyone—we've been trying for over a month. Given housing, planning and construction's role in air pollution, they should be here. On the record, we're not happy about that.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: I'm Diana Johnson, Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety at the Department of Health and Social Care.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I'm Chris Whitty, the Chief Medical Officer. I'm responsible for public health across Government, and I wrote an annual report on air pollution in 2022.

turns.speaker: Simon Reeve
turns.text: I'm Simon Reeve, deputy director for public health systems at DHSC. My team has policy responsibility for our interest in air pollution.

chapters.title: Health Impacts and Cross-Government Working
chapters.takeaway: Air pollution affects every stage of life and needs action across all departments, and although there are good relationships, a new Government review is a chance to improve coordination.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Diana, how easy is it for your Department to get other Government departments to take the health impacts of air pollution seriously?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: This is clearly a cross-Government issue—we can't leave it to Health or DEFRA alone. My Department provides the public health case and the evidence, like the link to 26,000 to 38,000 deaths a year and the cost to the NHS. We work with DEFRA and others. The air quality strategy review DEFRA has announced is a chance to look again at how Government works together.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Professor Whitty, can you take us through the key health impacts and causes?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Air pollution affects you throughout life—from premature birth and childhood asthma to heart disease, stroke, dementia, and some cancers. The Royal College of Physicians' central estimate is about 30,000 deaths a year, though that's an extrapolated figure. We've made progress: deaths used to be estimated at 40,000 a decade ago. If we act now, today's children could have much better lung health than any generation in two centuries.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The main causes are transport, construction, agriculture—especially ammonia, which hasn't really come down—and space heating. Anything that burns produces pollution, so electric heating is cleanest, then oil, then DEFRA-exempt wood burners, then old wood burners and open fires are worst.

chapters.title: What Would Make the Biggest Difference?
chapters.takeaway: International action, cleaner vehicles, agriculture changes and reducing indoor pollution in public buildings are among the most effective steps.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What key interventions would make the biggest difference?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: International action is really powerful—pollutants cross borders, and continent-wide vehicle standards drive down emissions without disadvantaging any country. Industry has made remarkable progress but construction is still tricky. We could also stop diesel engines idling in stations when there's a power source right there. And we should look at how countries like Holland cut ammonia from farming—it can be self-sustaining because farms use less fertiliser.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Our targets are less ambitious than WHO guidelines. Should policy move faster towards WHO levels, or are UK targets enough?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The WHO tightened its guidelines in 2021 because of new evidence. My view is we should push pollution as low as we can without wrecking the economy, and we can go a long way. Even if we hit UK targets, we should keep going because of the huge impact on chronic disease, child development and acute illness. I don't think that's controversial—most people would support it.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: If our legal limits still allow pollution linked to premature death and illness, what's the justification for keeping them?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: There are no safe targets, but DEFRA sets the targets and you'll hear from the DEFRA Minister next. The WHO says each nation must consider its own circumstances. The air quality strategy review will let us look at the latest health and scientific evidence when deciding what to do.

chapters.title: Inequality and Monitoring
chapters.takeaway: Air pollution hits deprived and vulnerable groups hardest, and better local data and measurement—including before-and-after studies—are needed to track progress.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Air pollution disproportionately affects children, deprived communities, ethnic minorities and those with existing health conditions. What progress is being made on those inequalities, and how are you measuring it?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: We're very aware of health inequalities. Our 10-year health plan aims to halve the gap in healthy life expectancy between richest and poorest. UKHSA has an air quality and health dashboard for England so local directors of public health can drill into their areas. The devolution Act puts a duty on mayoral combined authorities to look at health determinants. The CHILL study showed children's lungs can recover and grow with cleaner air—that's important for local policies like ULEZ. And the local outcomes framework includes an indicator on air pollution mortality.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Do you see monitoring as a local authority responsibility?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: They have a huge role, especially with devolution. But national and international responsibilities matter too. The concern isn't about devolving responsibility—it's about resources. I'm not an MHCLG Minister, but more money has gone into local government in the last two years, and local NHS joint strategic needs assessments help identify local health needs.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: People in deprived areas get a double hit: worse health and worse air pollution. The best approach is to reduce pollution for everyone—that has the biggest impact everywhere. On measurement, you can measure pollutants locally and work out where vulnerable populations are, but it's a calculated figure, not directly measured. That's why we should intervene in things we know will reduce pollution and measure before and after. As with CHILL, effects may be bigger than expected.

chapters.title: Doctors, Patients and Public Awareness
chapters.takeaway: Clinicians need better guidance on what to advise patients, and while there are already some public information tools, the committee questioned whether a national awareness campaign is needed.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: I met a nurse with TB recently who had no conversation about air quality with her respiratory consultant. TB rates are rising. Do clinicians have adequate guidance to communicate air pollution risks to patients?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I'm sorry to hear about your constituent. You're right that air pollution is a risk for TB and other respiratory infections. Most clinicians understand the risk, but the difficulty is advising individuals on what to do. Unlike smoking, where the advice is clear, air pollution is a generalised risk. Weather apps show pollution levels, and high-risk people can pay attention on high-pollution days. There's good guidance out there, and I've discussed it with the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and other CMOs. But the best thing societally is to reduce air pollution overall.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: The Chief Medical Officer has set that out well.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: Is current health surveillance and pollutant monitoring sufficient to track air pollution-related illnesses? What data is missing?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Air quality monitoring isn't bad but has technical limitations—the report goes into detail. Ideally we'd have a denser network, especially in urban areas where most risk is. We'd want close monitoring around schools, care homes and hospitals where vulnerable people are concentrated.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We know the greatest good is reducing pollution for all, but people living near busy roads are more vulnerable. Are we doing enough to identify and reduce risk for those most affected?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: You can see major roads picked out clearly on pollution maps. Reducing pollution for everyone is the biggest thing, but you're right that near major roads and airports you ideally wouldn't have the most vulnerable people. That's not my area, but the principle is clear.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: On outdoor pollution, there's genuine coordination across Government—DEFRA and Transport take it seriously. Indoor pollution is much less coordinated. As outdoor pollution has come down, indoor pollution's relative importance has grown, but our evidence base is weaker. I'd concentrate on public buildings—hospitals, libraries, supermarkets—because people have no choice but to go in them. That's an area where Government could be better coordinated.

chapters.title: Educating Doctors and Raising Public Awareness
chapters.takeaway: Medical training on air pollution is partway there, but the committee pushed for stronger national public messaging given the scale of the health burden.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: What action is being taken to ensure doctors are equipped to advise patients on air pollution risks, and by when will that be standard practice?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: It should be covered in medical school so all doctors get it. Some specialties—like general practice, paediatrics, obstetrics—need more. The royal colleges have done good work but could go further. The difficulty isn't saying there's a risk; it's saying what to do about it. If I had to put a number on it, maybe 50% of the way there—but there's quite a bit further to go.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Doctors are important, but other healthcare professionals like health visitors can also get information to families and children at risk.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Are integrated care systems required to identify and act on air pollution risks, or is it discretionary?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Integrated health plans have to identify local health needs. Integrated care includes commissioners, providers, DHSC and UKHSA. They work together at local level with councils and public health to assess needs and get information out.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Given air pollution is a major public health risk, should there be a specific national awareness campaign? We've done that for smoking, healthy eating, hot weather and covid. Why not for this silent killer?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: You have to be careful about communication. The daily air quality index has been updated, DEFRA runs alerts people can sign up to, and there's the Air Pollution Awareness Coalition. A range of things are happening. Whether we need to go further will be considered alongside DEFRA's air quality strategy review.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You're the Public Health Minister. Do you feel under pressure not to get the message out because it poses uncomfortable questions about housing, deprivation and other Government departments?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: No, I don't feel that at all. It's about using trusted healthcare professionals to give people advice—like we did during the hot weather. I'm not opposed to a more public awareness campaign if that's what we decide. We need to provide good information, cost-effectively, using all avenues to reach people. We'll look at what you recommend in your report.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But you're not saying yes to a campaign, and you're not saying no. Should you be doing more?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: It's not in my gift to announce that today. We'll look at your recommendations and be guided by the Chief Medical Officer's advice on communication. The Air Pollution Awareness Coalition has a strand on healthcare professionals, and we need to do more there. Whether we need something more public-facing is kept under review.

chapters.title: UK, International and Planning Perspectives
chapters.takeaway: England has the biggest air pollution problem in the UK, international examples like ammonia reduction offer lessons, and public health should have more input into planning decisions.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: What about coordination with Scotland and other parts of the UK, and learning from international examples?

turns.speaker: Simon Reeve
turns.text: DHSC is responsible for England, but UKHSA and COMEAP engage across the UK, so we're connected on the evidence.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I've discussed this with the other Chief Medical Officers. England has the biggest problem by far, especially southern England. Internationally, Holland and Canada have cut ammonia emissions by up to half through farming changes that become economically self-sustaining. Other countries have been imaginative about electrifying fleets in high-risk areas. There's a lot to learn.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: How well do you feel the Cabinet Office, Treasury and Business Department get these issues? There's often economic tension—like in Bradford and Manchester's clean air zone.

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: This can't be left to one, two or three departments—it has to be across Government. All departments signed up to the 10-year health plan, which has a section on air pollution. I'm keen to redouble efforts and make the public health case. On Manchester, the decision was made locally to invest in low-emission and electric buses instead of a ULEZ-type model. That's devolution—different solutions in different areas, but the same goal of reducing air pollution.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Should regional or local public health bodies be statutory consultees on planning applications? In my constituency, houses were built very close to a new bypass without any discussion of pollution levels. Given the Government's plan to build 1.5 million houses, should public health play a more fundamental role?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: Our public health directors do an excellent job. I'm happy to take that suggestion away and look at it. Local authorities and public health directors have an important role in reducing air pollution and improving health.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: I'd be keen to have as many opportunities as possible for educated public health input in planning decisions—it helps local decision makers have the full range of views. Whether it should be statutory is a political question, but if you were a local leader, you'd want that input to make an informed decision.

chapters.title: Ella's Law, Targets and the Road Ahead
chapters.takeaway: The panel acknowledged progress but emphasised that much more is needed, and questions about legal targets and new bills are for Ministers and Parliament.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: What's your view of the proposed Clean Air (Human Rights) Bill—Ella's law—which would establish a right to clean air and has wide cross-party support?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: Ella's tragic death has been an enormous spur to action, and her mother is here today—she's been a tireless and effective campaigner. But I'm going to dodge the question of whether a Bill is the right way, because that's for political leaders, not me. The general principle that we should drive change as a result of Ella's experience is clearly right.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Why haven't we followed the EU in updating limit values to reflect WHO guidelines? In 2008 we did that. Northern Ireland is looking at halving PM10 and cutting PM2.5 from 25 to 10. Isn't it strange that citizens in one part of the country are protected to a higher standard?

turns.speaker: Dame Diana Johnson
turns.text: You'll want to put that to Minister Hardy—DEFRA is responsible for targets. The air quality strategy review will look at all of that.

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: My job is to make the medical case that going further is essential. I've said we should keep going quite a long way across many sectors. But what the guidance should be is for Ministers, especially DEFRA Ministers. I won't give a view on that.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: Can you confirm the range of excess deaths attributable to air pollution?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: The central estimate is around 30,000 deaths a year—an extrapolated figure, not measured. But there's also a huge burden of ill health: premature birth, dementia, cardiovascular and lung disease, some cancers. That's why we want major changes—deaths are only part of it.

turns.speaker: Barry Gardiner
turns.text: We debate 250 knife crime deaths and 2,500 road deaths extensively, yet 30,000 from air pollution—we haven't moved, have we?

turns.speaker: Professor Sir Chris Whitty
turns.text: We have moved—the estimate was 40,000 a decade ago because pollution improved in many areas. But we can go further, and technically it's easy, though not straightforward in every sector. Reducing pollution would cut ill health, improve children's development and delay chronic disease. The arguments are clear. It doesn't happen by magic—it happens because Parliament pushes, laws change and engineers do better. We have made progress, and we can keep going down the slope.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Minister, Professor Whitty and Mr Reeve for your evidence. We're grateful for your appearance. That closes the first panel.
